Initially, the hardness was approximately 525 HV. By 6 h, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy achieved a remarkable Vickers hardness of 675 Hv.

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: Elemental powders of Co (99.8%), Cr (99.7%), Fe (99.96%), Ni (99.5%), and Ti (99.95%) in equimolar proportions. Intervention: Mechanical alloying (MA) for 6 hours. Processing: Planetary ball mill (QM-1SP4), stainless steel vessel/balls (5-10 mm), 20:1 ball-to-mill weight ratio, 400 rpm, argon atmosphere. Test conditions: Room temperature milling. Structure change: Formation of nanocrystalline solid solution with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% FCC and 17% BCC phases; disappearance of pure element peaks. Property change: Vickers hardness increased from approximately 525 HV (at 1 h) to 675 HV (at 6 h). Mechanism: Grain refinement and enhanced dislocation density due to prolonged milling. Evidence: measured. Quote: "The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases."

item.intervention: Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1000 °C for 10 minutes
item.processing: SPS in vacuum, graphite mold (30.4 mm diameter), heating rate 50 °C/min, hold time 10 min
item.structure_change: Bulk alloy formation with fine-grained microstructure; intergranular fracture observed
item.property_change: Compressive strength of 1894 MPa and yield stress of 1238 MPa achieved at 1000 °C
item.attributed_mechanism: Fine-grained microstructure and solid solution strengthening effects
quotes: Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa.
The curve indicated that the alloy achieved maximum strength of 1894 MPa and yield stress of 1238 MPa at 1000 °C.
The current material exhibited a fine–grained microstructure, similar to that observed in previous high–entropy alloys (HEAs), which enhanced its strength.

Following 4 h of mechanical alloying, the original elements of the high–entropy alloy gradually dissolved, leading to the formation of the solid solution.
According to the Williamson–Hall relationship, prolonged milling reduces crystal size while simultaneously increasing lattice strain.

item.structure_change: Reduction in micropores and increase in density as temperature rises

A higher sintering temperature can enhance the compaction rate, but there may be a saturation effect at very high temperatures.

item.property_change: Enhanced hardness compared to commercial alloys like Stellite (500 Hv)
item.attributed_mechanism: High titanium content induced lattice expansion
quotes: The bulk CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy exhibited superior microhardness compared to commercial alloys like Stellite (500 Hv) and nickel/cobalt–based superalloys.
The enhanced hardness can be attributed to the high titanium content, which induced lattice expansion.
This elevated hardness can be attributed to the refined microstructure, solid solution strengthening effects, and the significant proportion of the BCC phase within the alloy.

item.structure_change: Particle size reduced to approximately 30 ± 5 µm; formation of supersaturated solid solutions
item.attributed_mechanism: Fracture process dominance over cold welding; severe cold deformation
quotes: Extending the milling time to 6 h ( Figure 3 f) led to further particle crushing and yielded even finer particles, reducing the average size to approximately 30 ± 5 µm.
The intense collisions during the process induced significant cold working and work hardening effects in the particles, leading to a decrease in the average particle size.
The diminishing average particle size over prolonged milling periods underscores the dominance of the fracture process over cold welding.

item.structure_change: Presence of micropores due to suppressed atomic diffusion
item.property_change: Measured density of 6.57 g/cm³, much lower than theoretical density
item.attributed_mechanism: Suppression of atomic diffusion at low temperatures leading to decreased interaction between powder particles
quotes: When the sintering temperature is 950 °C, the measured density of the alloy is much lower than the theoretical density with 6.57 g/cm 3 .
Due to the suppression of atomic diffusion at low temperatures, there is a decrease in the interaction between powder particles during the sintering process.
The weakening of the bonding strength led to an increase in the number of micropores, ultimately reducing the density of the alloy.

item.structure_change: Emergence of hexagonal close–packed (HCP) structure peaks at 2θ angles of approximately 40° and 56°
item.attributed_mechanism: Presence of Ti with high melting point and largest atomic radius facilitating HCP lattice formation
quotes: After 3 h of mechanical alloying, the XRD pattern ( Figure 1 ) highlighted the emergence of two peaks at 2θ angles of approximately 40° and 56°, corresponding to the hexagonal close–packed (HCP) structure.

This phase formation was likely linked to the presence of Ti, which has a relatively high melting point and the largest atomic radius among the elements, facilitating the formation of an HCP crystalline lattice.
These two crystalline phases remained stable within the solid solution until the milling duration reached 6 h.

item.property_change: Compaction rate increased with sintering temperature

The compaction rate increased with the sintering temperature for all three samples.

This was consistent with the fundamental principles of sintering, where higher temperatures provide more energy for particle rearrangement, diffusion, and bonding, thereby accelerating the densification process.
